extracted.intended_audience: college and university faculty, department chairs, and higher-education administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and recommended practices for designing, administering, interpreting, and using teaching evaluations (student surveys, peer review, portfolios) across higher-education institutions. Emphasizes faculty role, multiple measures, timing, confidentiality, and protections for contingent faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty primacy in evaluation design and use
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary role of the faculty in teaching evaluation; faculty in the field should determine components and processes of teaching evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions made with little or no faculty involvement (e.g., shifting to online forms without faculty input) often have negative consequences. Chairs, deans, and provosts should familiarize themselves with AAUP statements; administrators should respect faculty-developed standards. Faculty should develop instruments and determine practices (peer review, classroom visits, teaching portfolios) that reflect course types, student levels, and teaching styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multifaceted / multiple-measures evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching evaluation should be a multifactored process including student evaluations, peer review, administrative review, teaching portfolios, mentoring, and other measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple parties (students, peers, administrators) and multiple instruments to reduce overreliance on any single metric and to counterbalance correlations between grades and student scores. Combine measures (peer review, portfolio, outcomes) and periodic meetings of instructors for comprehensive assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruments suited to field and pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of instruments that are suited to the field of knowledge and appropriate to the pedagogical methods used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating all teaching as the same; evaluation instruments must account for differences (large lecture vs small seminar). Faculty in the discipline should craft questions that reflect field standards and course formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid one-size-fits-all university-wide forms
rubrics_metrics.description: University-wide or college-wide evaluation forms that disregard variety in courses should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such forms generate meaningless numerical comparisons and invite misuse; department- or field-specific instruments are preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions should focus on student learning and be carefully worded
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation questions should focus on student learning and avoid wording that biases responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Do not ask 'Did the instructor return work in a timely manner?' but rather 'Did the instructor return work before the results were to be applied to a later assignment?' Include reflective components and midterm formative forms oriented toward learning effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and mode: in-class (paper) preferred to online outside class
rubrics_metrics.description: Student evaluations should be completed in class rather than online outside the classroom because online returns are much lower and less reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey found paper return rates of 80%+ vs online 20–40%, undermining claims of validity. Completing in class—even if anonymous—improves representativeness and may reduce extreme/abusive responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not allow evaluations after students know their grades
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluations should not be allowed after students have received their grades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing students to know their grades before evaluation undermines objectivity because stress and grade concerns at semester end influence responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality and restricted access to comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Confidentiality—anonymity of students completing evaluations and limits on who sees resulting comments—is essential to legitimate pedagogical purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While anonymity is important, some restrictions on who can view comments are needed. A majority favored some confidentiality protections; tracking anonymous responders to prevent multiple submissions was suggested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit publication and public availability of evaluation results
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing student evaluation results widely (beyond instructor, chair, dean) is counterproductive and should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: About 25% reported frequent publication; respondents largely opposed publication because it can be used like commercial rating sites and facilitate 'shopping' for easy classes. Institutions should not make numerical rankings publicly available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use student evaluations as the sole or primary indicator for personnel decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerically based student evaluations should not serve as the only or the primary indicator of teaching quality for promotion, tenure, or merit decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondents urged that teaching be evaluated as seriously as research, but with multiple measures; administrations should avoid overreliance on numerical student scores and the misuse of evaluations for renewal/nonrenewal of contingent faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat evaluations as formative (faculty development) rather than purely summative
rubrics_metrics.description: Course evaluations should be interpreted as faculty-development tools—formative rather than summative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret evaluations in course context, account for research on biases, and use them to improve teaching instead of imposing conformity or punitive measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include peer review and expert colleagues in evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer evaluation by colleagues with subject expertise and knowledge of field standards should be part of assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review and departmentally established grading norms can counterbalance student evaluations; peers can assess content standards and achievement expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop and use teaching portfolios and reflective materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching portfolios with a range of materials showing standards set by the instructor should be developed and used in evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portfolios can include syllabi, assignments, reflective statements, sample student work, evidence of learning outcomes, and can complement student evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentoring and mentoring programs for junior and contingent faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide mentoring and mutual mentoring programs for junior, non-tenure-track, and graduate-student instructors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondents strongly recommended mentoring and found it important to support teaching quality, especially since non-tenure-track faculty often receive less support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable support and inclusion for non-tenure-track and graduate instructors
rubrics_metrics.description: Graduate students and non-tenure-track faculty should have access to the same teaching development opportunities, peer evaluation, and mentoring offered to tenure-track faculty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of support exacerbates a two-tier system; contingent faculty face particular pressure to inflate grades and to prioritize student satisfaction over rigorous teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for and address abusive, discriminatory, or biased comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that anonymous online comments can have abusive/bullying tones and that women and faculty of color report discriminatory comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret comments with awareness of bias; ensure evaluation processes guard against discriminatory attacks and consider other evidence of teaching effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider return rates and representativeness when interpreting results
rubrics_metrics.description: Low return rates (especially online) and respondent composition compromise validity and representativeness of evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper in-class evaluations tend to include regular attendees; online responses may overrepresent extremes. Use this context when weighing numeric scores and comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret evaluations across multiple courses and semesters
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate an instructor by reviewing multiple courses taught over multiple semesters rather than a single snapshot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review trends, multiple courses, subsequent student performance in related courses, and include former students among evaluators to gain perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cross-evaluation and coordination for multisection courses
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodic meetings of instructors of multisection or related courses and cross-evaluation by other faculty can standardize expectations and improve reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meetings allow sharing of standards, common issues, and solutions; cross-evaluation helps align grading norms and pedagogical approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude certain students from evaluating (e.g., dropped or misconduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude students who have dropped a course or been charged with academic misconduct from evaluating the instructor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such exclusions aim to prevent uninformed or malicious evaluations; paper in-class evaluations make excluding dropouts easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using numerical evaluations to pressure grade inflation or lower standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrators should not exert pressure to obtain higher evaluation scores by lowering academic standards or imposing grade quotas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many respondents believed evaluations create upward pressure on grades; most opposed grade distribution quotas and publication of average grades that might encourage 'easy' teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about outcomes assessment as a sole improvement measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinions were split about the effectiveness of outcomes assessment in improving teaching; it should not be treated as a panacea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcomes assessment can be one tool, but respondents were evenly split on its efficacy; combine it with other measures and interpret carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor field-based pedagogical conferences and research over generic teaching centers
rubrics_metrics.description: Support instructors' participation in field-based pedagogical conferences and research on methods, rather than funding generic teaching centers alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although many institutions have teaching centers, respondents rarely praised them for promoting better pedagogy; field-based, discipline-specific development was preferred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight qualitative comments appropriately alongside quantitative scores
rubrics_metrics.description: Give more weight to qualitative components (student comments) rather than reducing evaluation to a numeric score alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerical evaluations are limited and can be misleading; comments, interpreted with caution for bias and context, provide richer evidence of teaching effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track and limit anonymous multiple submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: While anonymity is important, institutions should track anonymous responders to ensure no one completes an evaluation more than once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This proposal seeks to preserve anonymity while maintaining response integrity; implement technical or administrative safeguards as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure evaluation instruments and interpretation avoid bias and inappropriate uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation instruments and their use should account for known biases and avoid misuse, such as serving corporate governance aims or facilitating student selection of easy courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret scores with research on biases in mind; avoid reducing teaching to simple numeric comparisons used for marketing or punitive administration.
